questions.q: Let $A$ have rows $\langle1,2\rangle,\langle3,4\rangle$ and $B$ have rows $\langle0,-1\rangle,\langle2,1\rangle$. Find $A+B$ and $2A-B$.
questions.answer: $A+B$ has rows $\langle1,1\rangle,\langle5,5\rangle$. $2A$ has rows $\langle2,4\rangle,\langle6,8\rangle$, so $2A-B$ has rows $\langle2,5\rangle,\langle4,7\rangle$.

questions.q: Let $C$ have rows $\langle2,0,-1\rangle,\langle1,3,4\rangle$. Find $-3C$.
questions.answer: $-3C$ has rows $\langle-6,0,3\rangle,\langle-3,-9,-12\rangle$.

questions.q: Let $A$ have rows $\langle1,2\rangle,\langle3,4\rangle$ and $B$ have rows $\langle2,0\rangle,\langle1,3\rangle$. Find $AB$.
questions.answer: Row 1 of $AB$: $\langle1(2)+2(1),\ 1(0)+2(3)\rangle=\langle4,6\rangle$. Row 2: $\langle3(2)+4(1),\ 3(0)+4(3)\rangle=\langle10,12\rangle$. So $AB$ has rows $\langle4,6\rangle,\langle10,12\rangle$.

questions.q: For a $2\times3$ matrix $A$ and a $3\times2$ matrix $B$, what are the dimensions of $AB$? Is $BA$ defined, and if so, what dimension?
questions.answer: $AB$ is $2\times2$ (outer dimensions of $A$'s rows and $B$'s columns). $BA$ is also defined here (inner dimensions $2=2$ match), giving a $3\times3$ matrix — note $AB$ and $BA$ aren't even the same SIZE in general, let alone equal.

questions.q: Let $A$ have rows $\langle1,0,2\rangle,\langle-1,3,1\rangle$ (a $2\times3$ matrix) and $B$ have rows $\langle2,1\rangle,\langle0,1\rangle,\langle3,-1\rangle$ (a $3\times2$ matrix). Find $AB$.
questions.answer: Row 1 of $AB$: $\langle1(2)+0(0)+2(3),\ 1(1)+0(1)+2(-1)\rangle=\langle8,-1\rangle$. Row 2: $\langle-1(2)+3(0)+1(3),\ -1(1)+3(1)+1(-1)\rangle=\langle1,1\rangle$. So $AB$ has rows $\langle8,-1\rangle,\langle1,1\rangle$.

questions.q: For $A,B$ above (rows $\langle1,2\rangle,\langle3,4\rangle$ and $\langle2,0\rangle,\langle1,3\rangle$), compute $BA$ and compare it to $AB$.
questions.answer: Row 1 of $BA$: $\langle2(1)+0(3),\ 2(2)+0(4)\rangle=\langle2,4\rangle$. Row 2: $\langle1(1)+3(3),\ 1(2)+3(4)\rangle=\langle10,14\rangle$. So $BA$ has rows $\langle2,4\rangle,\langle10,14\rangle$ — different from $AB$'s rows $\langle4,6\rangle,\langle10,12\rangle$, confirming matrix multiplication is not commutative in general.

questions.q: Give one situation where $AB=BA$ IS guaranteed, even though matrix multiplication is not commutative in general.
questions.answer: If $B=I$ (the identity matrix) or, more generally, if $A=B$ (a matrix always commutes with itself), then $AB=BA$. Also, diagonal matrices of the same size always commute with each other.

sections.heading: The identity matrix and matrix inverses

questions.q: Describe the $2\times2$ and $3\times3$ identity matrices by their rows.
questions.answer: $I_2$: rows $\langle1,0\rangle,\langle0,1\rangle$. $I_3$: rows $\langle1,0,0\rangle,\langle0,1,0\rangle,\langle0,0,1\rangle$ — a $1$ down the main diagonal, $0$ everywhere else.

questions.q: Verify that $AI_2=A$ for $A$ with rows $\langle3,5\rangle,\langle2,1\rangle$.
questions.answer: Row 1: $\langle3(1)+5(0),\ 3(0)+5(1)\rangle=\langle3,5\rangle$. Row 2: $\langle2(1)+1(0),\ 2(0)+1(1)\rangle=\langle2,1\rangle$. So $AI_2$ has rows $\langle3,5\rangle,\langle2,1\rangle=A$, confirmed.

questions.q: For $A$ with rows $\langle a,b\rangle,\langle c,d\rangle$, state the formula for $A^{-1}$.
questions.answer: $A^{-1}$ is $\dfrac{1}{ad-bc}$ times the matrix with rows $\langle d,-b\rangle$ and $\langle-c,a\rangle$, provided $ad-bc\ne0$.

questions.q: Find the inverse of $A$ with rows $\langle3,1\rangle,\langle2,1\rangle$.
questions.answer: $\det A=3(1)-1(2)=1$. $A^{-1}$ has rows $\langle1,-1\rangle,\langle-2,3\rangle$. (Check: multiplying $A$ by this gives $I_2$.)

questions.q: Find the inverse of $A$ with rows $\langle2,5\rangle,\langle1,3\rangle$.
questions.answer: $\det A=2(3)-5(1)=1$. $A^{-1}$ has rows $\langle3,-5\rangle,\langle-1,2\rangle$.

questions.q: Use the inverse found above to solve the system $2x+5y=7$, $x+3y=4$ (writing it as $A\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{b}$ and computing $\mathbf{v}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$).
questions.answer: $A^{-1}$ has rows $\langle3,-5\rangle,\langle-1,2\rangle$, and $\mathbf{b}=\langle7,4\rangle$. $x=3(7)-5(4)=21-20=1$. $y=-1(7)+2(4)=-7+8=1$. Solution: $(x,y)=(1,1)$.

questions.q: State the formula for $(AB)^{-1}$ in terms of $A^{-1}$ and $B^{-1}$.
questions.answer: $(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$ (note the reversed order).

questions.q: If $A^{-1}$ has rows $\langle2,0\rangle,\langle1,1\rangle$ and $B^{-1}$ has rows $\langle1,1\rangle,\langle0,1\rangle$, find $(AB)^{-1}$.
questions.answer: $(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$. Row 1: $\langle1(2)+1(1),\ 1(0)+1(1)\rangle=\langle3,1\rangle$. Row 2: $\langle0(2)+1(1),\ 0(0)+1(1)\rangle=\langle1,1\rangle$. So $(AB)^{-1}$ has rows $\langle3,1\rangle,\langle1,1\rangle$.

questions.q: Explain briefly, using $(AB)(B^{-1}A^{-1})=I$, why the inverse of a product must reverse the order.
questions.answer: $(AB)(B^{-1}A^{-1}) = A(BB^{-1})A^{-1} = A I A^{-1} = AA^{-1} = I$ — the $B$'s and $B^{-1}$'s must sit adjacent to cancel, which only happens with the reversed order $B^{-1}A^{-1}$; the un-reversed guess $A^{-1}B^{-1}$ would not have matching factors cancel in the middle.

questions.q: For $A$ with rows $\langle1,2,3\rangle,\langle4,5,6\rangle$ (a $2\times3$ matrix), find $A^T$.
questions.answer: $A^T$ is $3\times2$ with rows $\langle1,4\rangle,\langle2,5\rangle,\langle3,6\rangle$ (the rows of $A$ become the columns of $A^T$).

questions.q: State the formula for $(AB)^T$ in terms of $A^T$ and $B^T$.
questions.answer: $(AB)^T=B^TA^T$ (transposing a product also reverses the order, just like inverses).

questions.q: A matrix $A$ is symmetric if $A^T=A$. Is the matrix with rows $\langle2,3\rangle,\langle3,5\rangle$ symmetric?
questions.answer: Yes: its transpose has rows $\langle2,3\rangle,\langle3,5\rangle$, identical to $A$ itself.

questions.q: For any matrix $A$, explain briefly why $A A^T$ is always symmetric, even when $A$ itself is not square.
questions.answer: $(AA^T)^T = (A^T)^T A^T = AA^T$ (using $(XY)^T=Y^TX^T$ and $(A^T)^T=A$), so $AA^T$ equals its own transpose — the defining property of a symmetric matrix.

questions.q: A diagonal matrix has rows $\langle3,0,0\rangle,\langle0,-2,0\rangle,\langle0,0,5\rangle$. Find its inverse (recall: the inverse of a diagonal matrix is diagonal, with reciprocal entries).
questions.answer: $D^{-1}$ has rows $\left\langle\dfrac{1}{3},0,0\right\rangle,\left\langle0,-\dfrac{1}{2},0\right\rangle,\langle0,0,\dfrac{1}{5}\rangle$.

questions.q: Multiply two diagonal matrices $D_1$ (rows $\langle2,0\rangle,\langle0,3\rangle$) and $D_2$ (rows $\langle5,0\rangle,\langle0,-1\rangle$). What pattern do you notice?
questions.answer: $D_1D_2$ has rows $\langle10,0\rangle,\langle0,-3\rangle$ — the product of two diagonal matrices is diagonal, with entries equal to the products of the corresponding diagonal entries.

questions.q: Explain why an upper triangular matrix (all entries below the main diagonal are zero) with a $0$ on its main diagonal cannot be invertible.
questions.answer: The determinant of a triangular matrix equals the product of its diagonal entries. If one diagonal entry is $0$, the whole product is $0$, so the determinant is $0$ — by the invertibility criterion, the matrix is singular.

questions.q: Is the sum of two upper triangular matrices always upper triangular? Is the sum of two symmetric matrices always symmetric? Justify each briefly.
questions.answer: Yes to both. Upper triangular: adding two matrices with zero entries below the diagonal keeps those entries zero. Symmetric: if $A^T=A$ and $B^T=B$, then $(A+B)^T=A^T+B^T=A+B$, so the sum is also symmetric.

questions.q: Find the inverse of the upper triangular matrix with rows $\langle2,3\rangle,\langle0,4\rangle$ using the $2\times2$ inverse formula, and confirm it is also upper triangular.
questions.answer: $\det=2(4)-3(0)=8$. $A^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{8}$ times the matrix with rows $\langle4,-3\rangle,\langle0,2\rangle$, i.e., rows $\left\langle\dfrac{1}{2},-\dfrac{3}{8}\right\rangle,\left\langle0,\dfrac{1}{4}\right\rangle$ — the lower-left entry is still $0$, so $A^{-1}$ is also upper triangular.
